item.content:encoded:
The Europe Defence and Security Fellowship 2027, hosted by Cranfield University at the Defence Academy of the United Kingdom in Shrivenham, offers a specialised opportunity for experienced professionals working in defence, security, government, law enforcement, intelligence, resilience, civil protection, and related international organisations.

Funded by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) and delivered by Cranfield University, the six-week fellowship is designed to strengthen the leadership, strategic decision-making, organisational resilience, cyber resilience, and emerging-technology capabilities of mid-career professionals from across Europe.

The programme brings together professionals who have demonstrated leadership potential and who have the ability to influence policy, strategy, organisational capability, or operational effectiveness within their organisations and countries.

Europe Defence and Security Fellowship 2027 at a Glance

  • Programme: Chevening Europe Defence and Security Fellowship
  • Host institution: Cranfield University
  • Host location: Defence Academy of the United Kingdom, Shrivenham
  • Funding: UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO)
  • Duration: Six weeks
  • Cohort 1: 25 January – 5 March 2027
  • Cohort 2: 15 March – 23 April 2027
  • Application deadline: 27 September 2026 at 11:00 UTC
  • Target applicants: Mid-career European professionals in defence, security, government, law enforcement, intelligence, civil protection, resilience, and international organisations
  • Programme format: Teaching, discussions, practical exercises, site visits, individual research, simulations, workshops, and collaborative learning

About the Europe Defence and Security Fellowship

The Chevening Europe Defence and Security Fellowship is designed for professionals who operate in environments where security and defence challenges are becoming increasingly complex and interconnected.

Modern security challenges can involve traditional defence concerns alongside cyber threats, artificial intelligence, emerging technologies, organisational vulnerabilities, governance challenges, and international cooperation.

The fellowship therefore takes an interdisciplinary and applied approach.

Rather than focusing on a single area of defence or security, participants will explore how leadership, organisational culture, governance, technology, resilience, and strategic decision-making interact.

The programme is intended to help fellows become more effective leaders who can operate within rapidly changing security and defence environments.

Participants will engage in:

  • Teaching and academic learning
  • Group discussions
  • Practical exercises
  • Workshops
  • Simulations
  • Practitioner-led sessions
  • Site and institutional visits in the United Kingdom
  • Individual research
  • Collaborative learning
  • International professional networking

A major component of the fellowship will be the opportunity to develop a research project addressing a relevant policy, leadership, organisational, or security challenge.

What Is the Aim of the Fellowship?

The programme aims to develop professionals who can operate effectively in complex security and defence environments.

Through the fellowship, participants will strengthen their ability to understand and respond to challenges affecting:

  • Governments
  • International organisations
  • Public institutions
  • Defence organisations
  • Security institutions
  • Civil protection systems
  • Resilience structures

The programme places particular emphasis on practical leadership and strategic thinking.

Fellows will be encouraged to examine problems from different perspectives and consider how decisions made under uncertainty can affect organisations, governments, and societies.

Six-Week Fellowship Programme

The fellowship lasts for six weeks and is offered through two cohorts in 2027.

Cohort 1

25 January – 5 March 2027

Cohort 2

15 March – 23 April 2027

Applicants should therefore consider which cohort best fits their professional circumstances when applying.

Key Learning Areas of the Europe Defence and Security Fellowship

The programme is organised around six integrated themes.

1. Global Leadership in an Era of Complexity

The first theme focuses on leadership within an increasingly complex international environment.

Security and defence professionals frequently need to make decisions while dealing with multiple stakeholders, competing interests, uncertainty, and rapidly changing circumstances.

Through this theme, fellows will examine leadership challenges and consider approaches for operating effectively in complex environments.

2. Understanding People, Culture, and Organisations

Security and defence organisations are influenced not only by policies and structures but also by people, organisational culture, behaviour, and governance.

This theme examines how these factors can influence:

  • Institutional effectiveness
  • Organisational resilience
  • Vulnerability
  • Decision-making
  • Leadership
  • Organisational performance

Understanding organisational culture and human behaviour can help leaders identify both strengths and vulnerabilities within their institutions.

3. Cyber Resilience and Information Threats

Cybersecurity and information threats are increasingly important components of national and international security.

The fellowship will provide fellows with an opportunity to explore cyber resilience and understand the challenges associated with information threats.

Participants will consider how organisations can better understand and respond to emerging cyber-related risks.

This theme is particularly relevant to professionals whose responsibilities involve security policy, resilience, defence, intelligence, technology, or organisational risk.

4. Artificial Intelligence, Governance, and Emerging Technology

Artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies are changing the way organisations operate and make decisions.

At the same time, these technologies create new governance, security, and ethical challenges.

The fellowship will examine both the opportunities and risks associated with artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and emerging technologies.

Participants will be encouraged to consider how governments and organisations can respond to technological change while maintaining effective governance and resilience.

5. Strategic Decision-Making Under Pressure

Security and defence professionals may be required to make important decisions in circumstances characterised by:

  • Uncertainty
  • Incomplete information
  • Competing pressures
  • Rapidly changing conditions

The fellowship will explore strategic decision-making approaches that can help professionals respond effectively in such environments.

The focus is not simply on making decisions, but on understanding the conditions under which strategic decisions are made and the factors that can influence their effectiveness.

6. Building Resilience and Future Leadership

The final theme brings together the fellowship’s emphasis on resilience and leadership.

Participants will explore how organisations can prepare for future challenges while developing leaders who can operate effectively in changing environments.

This theme connects leadership development with organisational resilience and the ability to anticipate and respond to future security challenges.

What Will Fellows Do During the Programme?

The Europe Defence and Security Fellowship uses a variety of learning methods rather than relying exclusively on classroom teaching.

Participants will have opportunities to engage in:

Lectures

Fellows will receive structured academic and professional input covering the programme’s major themes.

Workshops

Workshops will provide opportunities to explore issues in greater depth and apply concepts to practical situations.

Simulations

Practical simulations will allow fellows to engage with scenarios that reflect complex decision-making environments.

Practitioner Speakers

Fellows will hear from practitioners and professionals with relevant experience in defence, security, leadership, policy, and related areas.

Research Activity

Each fellow will work on an individual research project addressing a relevant challenge.

UK Institutional Visits

The programme includes visits to relevant institutions in the United Kingdom, providing participants with additional opportunities to understand institutional practices.

Collaborative Learning

Participants will learn alongside professionals from different European countries and professional backgrounds, creating opportunities for the exchange of ideas and experiences.

Fellowship Research Project

A significant component of the programme is the individual research project.

Throughout the fellowship, participants will work on a research project addressing a relevant:

  • Policy challenge
  • Leadership challenge
  • Organisational challenge
  • Security challenge

Fellows will receive academic support while developing their research.

At the conclusion of the programme, participants will have the opportunity to present their findings to the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) in London.

This gives fellows an opportunity to connect their research to real-world policy and institutional challenges.

International Networking Opportunities

Another important aspect of the Europe Defence and Security Fellowship is professional networking.

The programme brings together professionals from across Europe and the UK, creating opportunities to establish relationships across:

  • Countries
  • Professional sectors
  • Government institutions
  • Security organisations
  • Defence communities
  • International organisations

The fellowship is designed to create enduring professional networks that can continue beyond the six-week programme.

For professionals working in security and defence, these international relationships can be valuable for exchanging knowledge, experiences, and perspectives on shared challenges.

Who Can Apply for the Europe Defence and Security Fellowship?

The fellowship is specifically intended for mid-career professionals from eligible European countries who demonstrate leadership potential in security and defence.

Applicants must meet the programme’s additional eligibility requirements as well as the standard Chevening eligibility criteria.

Citizenship and Residency Requirement

At the point of application, applicants must be citizens of and residents in one of the following countries:

  • Andorra
  • Austria
  • Belgium
  • Bulgaria
  • Croatia
  • Cyprus
  • Czechia
  • Denmark
  • Estonia
  • Finland
  • France
  • Germany
  • Gibraltar
  • Greece
  • Holy See
  • Hungary
  • Iceland
  • Ireland
  • Italy
  • Latvia
  • Liechtenstein
  • Lithuania
  • Luxembourg
  • Malta
  • Monaco
  • Netherlands
  • Norway
  • Poland
  • Portugal
  • Romania
  • San Marino
  • Slovakia
  • Slovenia
  • Spain
  • Sweden
  • Switzerland

Applicants living in a European overseas territory may apply through the relevant Chevening award scheme for the European country of which they are a citizen.

Academic and Professional Requirements

In addition to meeting the standard Chevening eligibility criteria, applicants must meet several fellowship-specific requirements.

Postgraduate Qualification

Applicants must hold a postgraduate qualification, or have equivalent professional training or experience in a relevant field.

Professional Experience

Applicants must have at least five years of relevant professional experience.

This makes the fellowship particularly suitable for experienced professionals rather than recent graduates or early-career applicants.

Relevant Professional Sector

Applicants must be mid-career professionals employed within areas such as:

  • Government
  • Defence
  • Security
  • Law enforcement
  • Intelligence
  • Civil protection
  • Resilience
  • International organisations with responsibilities for national or international security

Leadership Potential

Applicants must be able to demonstrate leadership potential.

The fellowship is aimed at professionals who have the potential to contribute to organisational and national security-related priorities through their leadership.

Ability to Influence

Applicants should be working in roles that have the potential to influence:

  • Organisational capability
  • Policy
  • Strategy
  • Operational effectiveness

This influence may be within the applicant’s organisation and/or country.

Commitment After the Fellowship

Applicants must demonstrate a commitment to applying the knowledge, experience, and professional networks gained through the fellowship after completing the programme.

This means applicants should be able to explain how the fellowship could contribute to their future professional work and wider organisational or national impact.

Funding and Benefits

The fellowship provides financial support to successful participants.

According to the provided information, each fellowship includes:

Full Programme Fees

The fellowship covers the full programme fees.

Living Expenses

Fellows receive living expenses for the duration of the fellowship, including pre-arranged accommodation close to Oxford, as stated in the provided programme information.

Return Economy Airfare

The fellowship also includes return economy airfare.

These provisions are intended to support fellows throughout their participation in the six-week programme.

Why This Fellowship Is Relevant to Today’s Security Environment

Security and defence professionals increasingly need to understand issues beyond traditional security structures.

A contemporary security environment can involve interconnected challenges relating to:

  • Cybersecurity
  • Artificial intelligence
  • Emerging technologies
  • Organisational resilience
  • Governance
  • Human behaviour
  • Leadership
  • Information threats
  • International cooperation
  • Strategic decision-making

The fellowship’s interdisciplinary structure reflects this broader environment.

By bringing these subjects together, the programme aims to help professionals develop a more comprehensive understanding of the challenges faced by modern governments, organisations, and institutions.

Application Deadline

Applications for the Europe Defence and Security Fellowship are open until:

27 September 2026 at 11:00 UTC

Applicants should ensure that their application is submitted before the stated deadline.

Late applications may not be considered, so prospective applicants should allow sufficient time to review the eligibility criteria and prepare their application.

How to Apply

Eligible applicants can apply through the official Chevening application system.

Apply for the Europe Defence and Security Fellowship

Before applying, prospective candidates should carefully review both the standard Chevening eligibility requirements and the additional requirements for the Europe Defence and Security Fellowship.

What Makes a Strong Candidate for This Fellowship?

Based on the requirements provided, a strong candidate would be someone who can demonstrate several important characteristics.

1. Relevant Professional Experience

The applicant should have substantial experience in a relevant security, defence, government, resilience, law enforcement, intelligence, civil protection, or international organisation environment.

2. Leadership Potential

Applicants should demonstrate that they have the potential to become or continue developing as influential leaders within their professional environment.

3. Strategic Responsibilities

The applicant’s current position should provide opportunities to influence policy, strategy, organisational capability, or operational effectiveness.

4. Understanding of Security Challenges

Applicants should be able to demonstrate an understanding of contemporary security and defence challenges relevant to their work.

5. Future Application of Knowledge

Candidates should clearly demonstrate how they intend to apply the knowledge and networks gained during the fellowship after returning to their organisation or country.

Important Information for Applicants

The Europe Defence and Security Fellowship is a specialised programme with specific professional requirements.

It is therefore important for applicants to distinguish between simply having an interest in defence or security and actually meeting the programme’s professional eligibility requirements.

The fellowship specifically targets mid-career professionals whose current employment and responsibilities are connected to security, defence, resilience, government, law enforcement, intelligence, civil protection, or relevant international organisations.

Applicants should also pay attention to the requirement concerning the ability to influence organisational capability, policy, strategy, or operational effectiveness.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Europe Defence and Security Fellowship?

The Europe Defence and Security Fellowship is a six-week Chevening fellowship funded by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office and delivered by Cranfield University at the Defence Academy of the United Kingdom in Shrivenham.

How long does the fellowship last?

The fellowship lasts for six weeks.

When are the 2027 cohorts?

There are two cohorts:

  • Cohort 1: 25 January – 5 March 2027
  • Cohort 2: 15 March – 23 April 2027

Who is the fellowship designed for?

It is designed for mid-career professionals from eligible European countries who have demonstrated leadership potential in defence and security.

Do I need a postgraduate qualification?

Yes. Applicants must hold a postgraduate qualification or have equivalent professional training or experience in a relevant field.

How much professional experience is required?

Applicants must have at least five years of relevant professional experience.

Can professionals working in law enforcement apply?

Yes. Law enforcement is among the professional sectors specifically identified in the eligibility requirements.

Can intelligence professionals apply?

Yes. Intelligence professionals are included among the eligible professional profiles.

Can government employees apply?

Yes. Government professionals working in relevant security and defence contexts can apply, subject to meeting all other eligibility requirements.

Is the fellowship funded?

Yes. The provided information states that the fellowship includes full programme fees, living expenses including pre-arranged accommodation close to Oxford, and return economy airfare.

What is the application deadline?

The application deadline is 27 September 2026 at 11:00 UTC.

Is the fellowship open worldwide?

No. The provided eligibility requirements specify citizenship and residency in particular European countries. Applicants must also meet the programme’s professional and academic requirements.

Visit HERE for more information about the Europe Defence and Security Fellowship.

Conclusion

The Europe Defence and Security Fellowship 2027 offers a specialised six-week professional development experience for mid-career European professionals working in defence, security, government, law enforcement, intelligence, civil protection, resilience, and relevant international organisations.

Delivered by Cranfield University at the Defence Academy of the United Kingdom and funded by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, the programme combines academic learning with practical exercises, simulations, workshops, institutional visits, research, practitioner engagement, and international networking.

Its six core themes cover global leadership, organisational culture, cyber resilience, artificial intelligence and emerging technology, strategic decision-making, and future leadership and resilience. Fellows will also undertake an individual research project and present their findings to the FCDO in London at the end of the fellowship.

The opportunity is particularly suited to professionals who already have substantial experience and responsibilities within the defence and security environment and who can demonstrate the potential to influence policy, strategy, organisational capability, or operational effectiveness.

Eligible professionals should take note of the 27 September 2026 at 11:00 UTC application deadline and carefully assess the programme’s citizenship, residency, academic, professional, and leadership requirements before submitting an application.

item.content:encoded:
The University of Oxford has launched the Nuffield Medical Fellowships, a new research fellowship programme designed to support exceptional early-career researchers who are transitioning to independent research careers or who have recently established full research independence.

Established in 2026, the Nuffield Medical Fellowships provide an opportunity for outstanding biomedical researchers to develop and lead ambitious research programmes within the Medical Sciences Division of the University of Oxford. The programme is particularly significant for researchers whose work has the potential to advance medical knowledge and generate outcomes that improve human physical or mental health.

A distinctive feature of the fellowship is its international and collaborative dimension. Applicants must propose a research programme that includes a collaborative link with a research institution located in a Commonwealth country outside the United Kingdom. This requirement creates an opportunity for researchers to build meaningful international partnerships while conducting high-level medical research at Oxford.

The inaugural cohort will support two Fellows, with successful candidates expected to take up their fellowship positions in early 2028.

About the Nuffield Medical Fellowships

The Nuffield Medical Fellowships were established in 2026 by the Nuffield Medical Trust to support researchers with outstanding potential at an important stage of their academic careers.

The programme is aimed at researchers who are moving toward, or have recently achieved, full research independence. Rather than focusing solely on established senior researchers, the fellowship is intended to provide substantial support to researchers who are capable of developing and leading an ambitious programme of independent medical research.

Successful Fellows will be hosted by a suitable department within Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division. During the selection process, applicants will be matched with a department that can provide an appropriate academic and research environment for their proposed programme.

The fellowship is designed to provide both career support and research funding, enabling successful candidates to dedicate themselves to developing a substantial programme of medical research.

What Does the Nuffield Medical Fellowship Fund?

The Nuffield Medical Fellowships are intended to provide robust financial support for both the Fellow and the proposed research programme.

Each Fellowship will provide:

  • A full salary for the Fellow, in line with the appropriate University of Oxford staff grade.
  • Generous funding for the research programme.
  • The opportunity to conduct independent biomedical research within Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division.
  • An academic environment in which Fellows can develop their research programme and collaborate with researchers across disciplines.
  • Opportunities to establish or strengthen international research partnerships through the required Commonwealth-country collaboration.
  • Support for research aimed at advancing medical knowledge and improving human physical or mental health.

The combination of salary support and research funding makes the programme substantially different from opportunities that provide only a research stipend or limited project funding.

Who Can Apply for the Nuffield Medical Fellowship?

The fellowship is intended for exceptional early-career researchers who are either transitioning to full research independence or have recently achieved full research independence.

Applicants are expected to demonstrate outstanding research potential and submit a compelling proposal that clearly establishes the significance and potential impact of their proposed work.

The programme is open to both:

  • Practicing clinicians, and
  • Non-clinical researchers.

This means that applicants do not necessarily need to be practicing medical doctors. Researchers from appropriate biomedical and medical research backgrounds can also be considered, provided their proposed research meets the fellowship’s requirements.

Eligible Research Areas

One of the important features of the Nuffield Medical Fellowship is the breadth of research fields that can be considered.

The proposed research must be in a biomedical field and should seek to advance medical knowledge in a way that is expected to benefit human physical or mental health.

Eligible areas include:

  1. Clinical medicine
  2. Surgery
  3. Neuroscience
  4. Epidemiology
  5. Population health
  6. Primary care
  7. Physiology
  8. Biochemistry
  9. Pharmacology
  10. Psychiatry
  11. Experimental psychology

The programme is therefore relevant to researchers working across a broad spectrum of medical and biomedical disciplines.

Applicants should ensure that their proposed research is clearly connected to medical advancement and has a credible pathway toward improving human health.

International Collaboration Requirement

A particularly important eligibility feature is the requirement for an international research collaboration.

The proposed research programme must involve a collaborative link with a research institution based in a Commonwealth country outside the UK.

This means that applicants need to demonstrate more than an interest in international research. Their proposed programme must incorporate a meaningful collaborative relationship with an eligible research institution located in a Commonwealth country outside the United Kingdom.

This element of the programme can be particularly relevant to researchers whose work addresses global health, population health, health inequalities, infectious diseases, environmental health, clinical research, public health, or other areas where international collaboration can strengthen research outcomes.

Applicants should therefore consider carefully how their proposed partnership contributes to the research programme rather than treating the collaboration as an additional or separate component.

Research Proposal Expectations

A strong research proposal is central to the Nuffield Medical Fellowship application.

Applicants are expected to submit a compelling research proposal that demonstrates how their work will advance medical knowledge.

The proposal should therefore clearly communicate the research problem, the proposed approach and the expected contribution of the research.

When developing a proposal, applicants should be prepared to explain:

  • The medical or biomedical problem being addressed.
  • The research question or questions.
  • Why the research is important.
  • The existing knowledge or evidence surrounding the problem.
  • The proposed research approach.
  • How the research will contribute to advancing medical knowledge.
  • The expected outcomes of the research.
  • How those outcomes could contribute to improvements in human physical or mental health.
  • The applicant’s capacity to lead the research independently.
  • The role of the proposed Commonwealth-country research collaboration.
  • Why the University of Oxford provides an appropriate environment for the proposed programme.

The proposal should also demonstrate a clear connection between the applicant’s research trajectory and the programme they intend to establish at Oxford.

University of Oxford Medical Sciences Division

Successful Fellows will be hosted within the Medical Sciences Division of the University of Oxford.

The Medical Sciences Division brings together a wide range of medical and biomedical research departments and provides an environment for interdisciplinary research.

As part of the fellowship selection process, applicants will be matched with an appropriate department that can host their proposed research programme.

This means that applicants should consider how their research aligns with the expertise, facilities and research environment available within Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division.

The institutional fit is particularly important because the fellowship is intended to support a substantial research programme rather than a short-term research placement.

Number of Fellowships Available

For the inaugural cohort, the Nuffield Medical Trust is providing funding for two Fellowships.

The first Fellows are expected to take up their positions in early 2028.

The programme is also intended to become an ongoing annual fellowship scheme. Going forward, the Trustees expect to appoint approximately one to two Fellows each year through an annual recruitment round.

This makes the 2026 programme the first cohort of what is intended to become a continuing fellowship opportunity.

Who Is the Fellowship Suitable For?

The Nuffield Medical Fellowships may be particularly relevant to researchers who are at a career stage where they are moving from supervised or collaborative research toward independent leadership.

Potential applicants may include:

  • Early-career biomedical researchers.
  • Researchers who have recently achieved full research independence.
  • Researchers transitioning into independent research leadership.
  • Practicing clinicians with strong research programmes.
  • Non-clinical biomedical researchers.
  • Researchers working in clinical or translational medicine.
  • Researchers working in population health or epidemiology.
  • Neuroscience researchers.
  • Researchers in physiology, biochemistry or pharmacology.
  • Researchers working in psychiatry or experimental psychology.
  • Researchers whose work addresses human physical or mental health.
  • Researchers able to establish an appropriate collaborative relationship with an eligible Commonwealth-country research institution outside the UK.

Applicants should nevertheless assess their individual circumstances and the detailed application requirements before applying.

Countries and Nationalities: Who Can Apply?

The information provided by the University of Oxford describes the international collaboration requirement in terms of the location of the collaborating research institution, rather than restricting applicants to a particular nationality or race.

The key geographical requirement stated by the programme is that the proposed research must involve a collaborative link with a research institution based in a Commonwealth country outside the UK.

Therefore, the important distinction is between the applicant’s nationality and the location of the required research collaboration.

Researchers should consult the official fellowship application guidance for the complete eligibility requirements and any additional restrictions concerning applicants, host institutions or collaborating institutions.

The opportunity is not presented as being restricted to a particular race.

Why the Commonwealth Collaboration Matters

The international collaboration component gives the fellowship a distinctive global dimension.

Medical research increasingly depends on collaboration between institutions, researchers and health systems across different countries. Partnerships can provide access to different populations, research environments, expertise, datasets, clinical settings and scientific perspectives.

For researchers whose work has an international or global-health dimension, a collaboration with an institution in a Commonwealth country could strengthen the practical relevance and reach of the proposed programme.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate a substantive research rationale for the partnership and explain how the collaboration contributes to achieving the objectives of the proposed research.

Expected Research Impact

The Nuffield Medical Fellowships are designed around research that can make a meaningful contribution to medical knowledge.

The programme specifically requires research proposals to pursue outcomes expected to benefit human physical or mental health.

This means applicants should think beyond simply describing a technically interesting research question. They should also explain the broader significance of the research and how the expected findings could contribute to improved understanding, prevention, diagnosis, treatment, management or other aspects of human health, depending on the field.

The nature of the potential impact will naturally differ between disciplines. For example, an epidemiological project may generate evidence relevant to population health, while a neuroscience project could contribute to understanding neurological processes or disorders.

Career Development and Research Independence

One of the central purposes of the Nuffield Medical Fellowship is to support researchers at the transition to research independence.

For an early-career researcher, developing an independent research programme can require substantial resources, including salary support, research funding, institutional infrastructure, collaborators and an environment capable of supporting ambitious scientific work.

The Fellowship is structured to provide these elements together.

By funding the Fellow’s salary while also providing research programme funding, the scheme is designed to enable successful candidates to concentrate on developing and leading their research programme within Oxford.

How the Selection and Hosting Process Works

Applicants are expected to propose research that fits strategically with a department within the University of Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division.

During the selection process, applicants will be matched with a suitable department that will host their Fellowship.

This makes institutional alignment an important consideration when preparing an application.

Researchers should carefully consider the relationship between:

  • Their research expertise.
  • Their proposed research programme.
  • The scientific environment at Oxford.
  • The relevant Medical Sciences Division department.
  • Potential collaborators.
  • The Commonwealth-country institutional partnership.
  • The anticipated contribution of the research to medical knowledge and human health.

A coherent connection between these elements can help demonstrate why the proposed programme is suitable for the Fellowship.

How to Apply

Applicants interested in the Nuffield Medical Fellowships should review the official How to Apply information provided by the University of Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division.

The application process should be approached carefully because the programme is intended for researchers proposing substantial independent research programmes.

Applicants should review all application instructions, eligibility conditions, proposal requirements and supporting-document requirements before submitting their application.

It is also advisable to ensure that the proposed research programme is clearly developed before beginning the application, particularly where an international institutional collaboration is required.

Fellowship Timeline

The Nuffield Medical Fellowships were established in 2026, making this the programme’s inaugural recruitment cycle.

The first cohort will consist of two Fellows, and the inaugural Fellows are expected to begin their positions in early 2028.

The Trustees subsequently expect to appoint approximately one to two Fellows per year through an annual recruitment process.

Deadline

Applicants should check the official University of Oxford application page for the current application deadline, as the programme information supplied does not state a specific deadline.

Because recruitment dates can change, prospective applicants should rely on the official Oxford fellowship page and application portal for the authoritative deadline and submission instructions.

About the Funder: Nuffield Medical Trust

The Nuffield Medical Trust is the funder behind the Nuffield Medical Fellowships.

The Trustees have committed to establishing a robust and well-funded programme capable of supporting high-potential researchers and ambitious medical research programmes.

The funding commitment for the inaugural cohort includes support for two Fellows, with the programme intended to continue through future annual recruitment rounds.

Key Features of the Nuffield Medical Fellowship

The major features of the opportunity include:

  • Established in 2026.
  • Hosted by the University of Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division.
  • Designed for exceptional early-career researchers.
  • Supports researchers transitioning to or recently achieving full research independence.
  • Open to practicing clinicians and non-clinical researchers.
  • Research must be in a biomedical field.
  • Research must aim to advance medical knowledge.
  • Proposed outcomes should be expected to benefit human physical or mental health.
  • Eligible areas include clinical medicine, surgery, neuroscience, epidemiology, population health, primary care, physiology, biochemistry, pharmacology, psychiatry and experimental psychology.
  • Requires a collaborative link with a research institution in a Commonwealth country outside the UK.
  • Provides a full salary for the Fellow according to the appropriate University of Oxford staff grade.
  • Provides generous funding for the research programme.
  • Two Fellowships are available in the inaugural cohort.
  • Successful Fellows are expected to take up their positions in early 2028.
  • The Trustees expect to appoint one to two Fellows annually in future recruitment rounds.

Tips for Prospective Applicants

Researchers considering this fellowship should begin preparing well in advance.

1. Develop a clear independent research programme

The Fellowship is intended to support researchers moving into independent research leadership. Your proposal should therefore demonstrate that you have a coherent research vision rather than simply describing a single isolated study.

2. Clearly establish the medical significance

Explain why the research matters and how it can contribute to medical knowledge and, ultimately, human physical or mental health.

3. Build a meaningful international collaboration

Because collaboration with a Commonwealth-country institution outside the UK is a central programme requirement, applicants should carefully consider the institution and researchers with whom they intend to collaborate.

The partnership should have a clear scientific purpose and contribute directly to the proposed research programme.

4. Demonstrate research independence

Applicants should clearly communicate their research achievements, expertise, intellectual contribution and capacity to lead an independent programme.

5. Consider Oxford’s departmental fit

Think carefully about which area of Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division best aligns with the proposed research. The Fellowship includes a departmental hosting component, making institutional fit an important part of the overall application.

6. Explain expected outcomes

Avoid focusing exclusively on research methods. Explain what the research is expected to discover, develop or demonstrate and why those outcomes matter.

7. Check the official requirements

Before submitting an application, applicants should carefully review the official University of Oxford information, including the application instructions and frequently asked questions.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Nuffield Medical Fellowship fully funded?

The Fellowship provides a full salary for the Fellow in line with the appropriate University of Oxford staff grade, together with generous funding for the Fellow’s research programme.

How many Fellowships are available?

Two Fellowships are being supported in the inaugural cohort.

When will the successful Fellows begin?

The inaugural Fellows are expected to take up their positions in early 2028.

Is the Fellowship only for doctors?

No. The programme can support both practicing clinicians and non-clinical researchers, provided they meet the fellowship requirements and propose eligible biomedical research.

What research areas are eligible?

The programme covers a broad range of biomedical fields, including clinical medicine, surgery, neuroscience, epidemiology, population health, primary care, physiology, biochemistry, pharmacology, psychiatry and experimental psychology.

Does the research have to benefit human health?

Yes. The proposed research should aim to advance medical knowledge through outcomes expected to benefit human physical or mental health.

Is international collaboration required?

Yes. The proposed research programme must involve a collaborative link with a research institution based in a Commonwealth country outside the UK.

How many Fellows will be selected each year?

The inaugural cohort will have two Fellows. In subsequent years, the Trustees expect to appoint approximately one to two Fellows annually.

Where will the Fellow be hosted?

Successful applicants will be hosted by a suitable department within the University of Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division. Applicants will be matched to a department during the selection process.

Is there a stated application deadline?

The programme information provided does not specify a deadline. Applicants should consult the official Oxford application page for the current deadline and submission instructions.

Conclusion

The Nuffield Medical Fellowships at the University of Oxford offer a major research opportunity for exceptional early-career biomedical researchers who are ready to develop or have recently developed independent research programmes.

Established in 2026, the Fellowship combines salary support with substantial research programme funding and places successful researchers within Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division. The programme covers a wide range of biomedical disciplines, from clinical medicine, surgery and neuroscience to epidemiology, population health, pharmacology, psychiatry and experimental psychology.

A defining feature of the Fellowship is its international collaboration requirement. Applicants must develop a research programme that includes collaboration with a research institution in a Commonwealth country outside the United Kingdom. This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to researchers interested in building international research partnerships and addressing medical challenges through collaborative research.

The inaugural programme will support two Fellows, with successful candidates expected to begin in early 2028. With the Nuffield Medical Trust intending to continue the programme through annual recruitment rounds, the Fellowship is designed to provide sustained support for emerging research leaders and ambitious medical research programmes.

Researchers who meet the eligibility requirements and have a strong, independent biomedical research vision should review the official University of Oxford application guidance carefully, identify an appropriate departmental fit, develop a compelling research proposal and ensure that the required Commonwealth-country collaboration is meaningfully integrated into their programme.

item.content:encoded:
The Better Life Lab at New America is inviting journalists and storytellers to apply for its 2026–2027 Multimedia Reporting Grants, an opportunity designed to support powerful, solutions-oriented stories about caregiving, child care, family support, disability care, elder care, and end-of-life care.

The reporting grants are intended for storytellers who can use journalism and creative storytelling to explore the challenges surrounding care in the United States while highlighting practical solutions, innovations, and possibilities for building stronger care systems.

Selected storytellers will have their stories commissioned on a rolling basis beginning in October 2026. In addition to funding for reporting, successful applicants will be invited to participate in the Better Life Lab’s reporting cohort and receive editorial guidance and placement assistance.

The program welcomes both new and experienced reporters and particularly encourages applications from people with perspectives that have traditionally been underrepresented in the media.

About the Better Life Lab Multimedia Reporting Grants

The Better Life Lab, a program at New America, focuses on issues connected to work-family justice, gender equity, and the value of care.

The Lab recognizes that care is a universal part of human life. People provide or receive care in many different circumstances, including raising children, supporting family members during illness, caring for older relatives, assisting people with disabilities, and providing comfort at the end of life.

However, the source notes that care infrastructure in the United States faces significant challenges. The Better Life Lab therefore sees storytelling as an important way to examine these challenges, highlight solutions, influence policy discussions, and help audiences understand why care systems matter.

Through the 2026–2027 reporting grants, the Lab is seeking journalists and storytellers who can develop compelling stories that do more than describe problems. The program emphasizes reporting that identifies approaches that are already being tested or implemented and examines what could be learned from them.

What the 2026–2027 Reporting Grants Are Looking For

The Better Life Lab is particularly interested in stories addressing two major pillars of the care crisis:

1. Innovations in Child Care

One major focus of the reporting grants is innovation in child care.

Applicants are encouraged to develop stories about real-world efforts that are already underway and that could contribute to a more equitable and accessible child care system.

The goal is to identify and explore promising approaches while helping audiences envision what a stronger child care system could look like.

Stories in this area may examine child care solutions or address fundamental questions about how early childhood education and care can be improved.

The source specifically identifies several areas that storytellers can explore, including:

  • Rethinking when learning begins.
  • Examining who is served by child care systems.
  • Exploring the quality of care provided.
  • Examining the costs associated with child care.
  • Exploring how child care is financed and paid for.
  • Highlighting innovations that could contribute to a more equitable child care system.
  • Examining approaches that could provide families with greater choices.
  • Exploring ways of supporting living wages for child care educators and providers.

The initiative’s child care reporting component is supported by the Bainum Family Foundation and other funders.

Applicants interested in this area can therefore consider reporting that moves beyond identifying shortcomings and instead investigates programs, models, practices, policies, or community efforts that could offer useful lessons for the future.

2. Investments in Care Infrastructure

The second major focus is the broader issue of investment in care infrastructure.

This area recognizes that caregiving extends throughout the life cycle and is not limited to early childhood.

The Better Life Lab is seeking multimedia stories examining both challenges and potential solutions affecting caregivers and people who depend on care, including:

  • Infants and young children.
  • Families requiring child care.
  • People with disabilities.
  • Older adults.
  • Families caring for aging relatives.
  • People approaching the end of life.
  • Caregivers supporting family members across different stages of life.

The reporting can explore how investments in care infrastructure could strengthen families, communities, and gender equality.

The Lab’s call also points to the relationship between caregiving and women’s lives, noting that care is often treated as a private family responsibility and frequently falls disproportionately on women.

Stories can therefore examine how better care infrastructure could affect families and communities while also considering the broader economic and social implications of care.

Solutions-Oriented Journalism Is at the Heart of the Opportunity

A defining feature of these reporting grants is the emphasis on solutions-oriented storytelling.

Rather than focusing exclusively on what is broken within care systems, the Better Life Lab wants stories that investigate how and why care issues matter and what can be done about them.

The program describes its approach as solutions journalism: reporting that emphasizes not only problems but also possible ways of addressing them.

For applicants, this means that a strong reporting proposal should ideally have a clear connection between the issue being examined and potential solutions, innovations, or approaches that can be explored through reporting.

The stories should help audiences understand:

  1. Why care matters to families.
  2. Why care matters to children.
  3. Why care matters to communities.
  4. Why care matters to the economy.
  5. What innovative approaches are already being attempted.
  6. Whether particular innovations could be expanded or replicated.
  7. What a better future for care could look like.

The Better Life Lab says this approach is intended to help build the energy and public demand necessary to support solutions to care challenges.

Who Can Apply for the Reporting Grants?

The opportunity is open to journalists and storytellers, with applications welcomed from both new and experienced reporters.

The source specifically states that:

  • New reporters are welcome to apply.
  • Experienced reporters are welcome to apply.
  • People with perspectives traditionally underrepresented in the media are especially encouraged to apply.

The program is therefore not restricted solely to established journalists with long professional careers. The invitation explicitly includes newer reporters and storytellers.

What Types of Stories Can Be Submitted?

The Better Life Lab is open to a broad range of storytelling formats.

Applicants are not limited to conventional written journalism. The program welcomes multiple forms of media, including

  • Print stories.
  • Online articles.
  • Photojournalism.
  • Graphic stories.
  • Podcasts.
  • Audio stories.
  • Multimedia projects.
  • Videography.

The Lab also expresses interest in new and creative storytelling methods that can reach broad and diverse audiences.

This provides applicants with considerable flexibility in how they approach a proposed story. Rather than requiring every applicant to use the same medium, the program allows storytellers to select a format that fits the subject and intended audience.

Creative Storytelling and Reaching Diverse Audiences

The Better Life Lab is interested in stories that can communicate complex care issues to broad and diverse audiences.

Applicants should therefore consider how their proposed reporting can make care-related issues understandable, engaging, and relevant to people beyond a specialized professional audience.

Creative approaches may be particularly relevant where they help audiences understand:

  • The realities faced by caregivers.
  • The experiences of families seeking care.
  • The importance of child care systems.
  • The challenges associated with aging.
  • Disability and care needs.
  • End-of-life care.
  • The economic importance of care.
  • Innovative solutions being tested in communities.

The Lab also wants stories that can paint a vision of what is possible in the future and examine whether promising innovations have the potential to scale.

What Selected Storytellers Receive

Successful applicants will receive more than an opportunity to develop a story.

According to the Better Life Lab, selected journalists and storytellers will benefit from several forms of support.

Reporting Commissions

Stories will be commissioned on a rolling basis beginning in October 2026.

This means selected storytellers will have an opportunity to develop reporting around the care-related topics identified by the program.

Participation in a Reporting Cohort

Selected journalists will also be invited to participate in the Better Life Lab reporting cohort.

This creates an opportunity for participating storytellers to engage with others working on care-related reporting and become part of a broader group supported by the Lab.

Editorial Guidance

The program will provide selected journalists with editorial guidance.

This support can be particularly relevant for storytellers developing complex stories that require careful reporting, framing, research, and presentation.

Placement Assistance

Selected storytellers will also receive placement assistance.

The source indicates that the Lab works with its grantees to support the publication and placement of their stories.

Track Record of the Better Life Lab Reporting Grants

The Better Life Lab has an established history of supporting storytellers.

Since 2021, the Lab reports that it has supported more than 30 different storytellers.

Together with its team, it has produced nearly 100 stories on child care innovations, with those stories appearing in nearly 40 different publications and media outlets.

This previous work demonstrates the program’s focus on taking care-related reporting to established media audiences.

Examples highlighted by the Lab include stories published by outlets such as Slate, Wisconsin Examiner, and Vox.

The examples cover topics including elder care, child care differences across countries, and challenges facing caregivers who simultaneously support aging parents and children.

Previous Better Life Lab Care Story Collections

The Better Life Lab has also published collections of stories from previous reporting grant periods.

Applicants interested in understanding the type of work previously supported by the program can review its earlier collections, including:

  • 2023: Telling the Story of Child Care
  • 2024 and 2025: Collection of Stories on Care

These previous collections can provide useful context about the themes and approaches that have been explored through the reporting initiative.

Resources for Applicants and Reporters

The Better Life Lab also provides resources for journalists and storytellers interested in reporting on care.

One resource focuses specifically on telling stories of care through video.

The resource provides guidance for reporters who want to create videos, including practical considerations such as writing a script and preparing for presentation on camera.

Applicants interested in producing video or multimedia reporting may find these resources particularly relevant when developing their storytelling approach.

Why Caregiving Stories Matter

Caregiving affects virtually every stage of life.

Families may need child care when children are young, support for relatives dealing with illness, assistance for people living with disabilities, care for aging family members, or support during the end-of-life stage.

Because these needs affect individuals, families, communities, workplaces, and economies, reporting on care can extend beyond personal stories and examine wider social and economic systems.

The Better Life Lab’s reporting grants provide a platform for exploring these connections through journalism and creative storytelling.

The program’s emphasis on solutions also means that applicants can investigate not only the challenges people experience but also the initiatives attempting to address those challenges.

How to Apply for the 2026–2027 Better Life Lab Reporting Grants

Applications for the 2026–2027 Multimedia Reporting Grants are currently being accepted by the Better Life Lab.

Interested journalists and storytellers should submit their applications through the application form provided by the program.

Stories will be commissioned on a rolling basis beginning in October 2026, so applicants should review the official application information and submit their proposals through the designated application process.

Applicants should ensure that their proposed story clearly connects to the program’s focus on care, work-family justice, gender equity, child care, or care infrastructure.

A proposal should also demonstrate how the story can contribute to a solutions-oriented understanding of the issue.

Application Link

Interested applicants can access the official application form through the Better Life Lab’s reporting grant announcement.

The program’s official announcement is published by New America and contains the application form and additional information about the reporting grants.

APPLY HERE

Important Considerations Before Applying

Before submitting an application, prospective applicants should carefully consider whether their proposed story fits the program’s focus.

A strong proposal should consider the following questions:

  1. Does the story address care?
    The proposed reporting should connect clearly to caregiving, child care, disability care, elder care, end-of-life care, or care infrastructure.
  2. Is the story solutions-oriented?
    The program is particularly interested in reporting that examines potential solutions rather than focusing exclusively on problems.
  3. Is there a real-world innovation or approach to investigate?
    Stories about initiatives already underway may be particularly relevant, especially where they can demonstrate lessons for the future.
  4. Can the story reach a broad audience?
    The Lab welcomes creative approaches capable of helping diverse audiences understand why care matters.
  5. Could the innovation potentially scale?
    The program encourages stories that explore whether promising approaches can be expanded.
  6. Is the chosen medium appropriate for the story?
    Applicants can consider print, online reporting, photography, graphics, podcasts, audio, multimedia, or video depending on the proposed story.

Visit HERE for more information about the 2026–2027 Better Life Lab Multimedia Reporting Grants for Journalists and Storytellers.

Deadline and Timeline

The source does not provide a fixed application deadline for the 2026–2027 reporting grants.

Instead, the Better Life Lab states that applications are being accepted and that stories will be commissioned on a rolling basis beginning in October 2026.

Applicants should therefore consult the official application information for the most current submission details.

Conclusion

The 2026–2027 Better Life Lab Multimedia Reporting Grants provide journalists and storytellers with an opportunity to investigate some of the most important issues surrounding caregiving and care infrastructure through solutions-oriented journalism.

The program covers a broad range of subjects, from innovations in child care to disability, elder, family, and end-of-life care. It also welcomes diverse storytelling formats, including written journalism, photography, graphic stories, podcasts, audio, multimedia projects, and videography.

For selected storytellers, the opportunity extends beyond reporting support. Participants will be commissioned to produce stories, invited into the Better Life Lab reporting cohort, and provided with editorial guidance and placement assistance.

With more than 30 storytellers supported since 2021 and nearly 100 stories on child care innovations produced in collaboration with the Lab, the initiative has an established record of supporting care-focused journalism.

Journalists and storytellers interested in exploring practical solutions to challenges affecting families, caregivers, communities, and the wider economy can consider applying to the 2026–2027 reporting grant program. Since applications are accepted on a rolling basis and commissions begin in October 2026, prospective applicants should review the official application information and prepare proposals that clearly demonstrate the relevance, originality, and solutions-oriented nature of their proposed reporting.

For more global Grant opportunities, visit OFY HERE.

The post 2026–2027 Better Life Lab Multimedia Reporting Grants for Journalists and Storytellers appeared first on Opportunities for Youth.
